segments.t: Barinov has taken a spoonful of Max's pâté. Max is waiting for the compliment, and what he gets is not quite what he hoped for.
Let's replay it, with a word or two on each line.
'Not bad.' 'Neplokho' is one word: 'ne', 'not', joined to 'plokho', 'badly'. Russians use it for anything from 'fine' to 'quite good'.
'Really?' 'Da?' is literally 'yes?', but with a rising voice it means 'really?', so one syllable does the work of a whole question. Max is fishing for more praise.
'Only this isn't my pâté.' 'Tolko', 'only', also works as 'but' at the start of a sentence. The 'ne', 'not', goes right before the word it denies, here 'moy', 'my'.
'What? Same texture.' Max says 'kak?', literally 'how?', which is what Russians say when they are stunned. 'Ta zhe' means 'the same', and 'ta' is feminine to match 'konsistentsiya'.
'And I got the ingredients right.' 'Sostav', 'composition', is the word printed above the ingredients list on any packet. 'Podobral' means 'picked out' or 'matched'.
'Wait.' 'Podozhdite' is the polite 'wait', with the '-ite' ending for 'vy'. To a friend Max would say 'podozhdi'.
'What goes into your pâté?' Russian says the ingredients 'vkhodyat v', 'go into', a dish. 'Vash', 'your', goes with 'vy'.
'Let's go and take a look.' 'Poydyom posmotrim', literally 'we'll go, we'll look', needs no 'and' between the verbs. Barinov says it instead of answering. Let's finish by hearing it all again.
Max thought he had won, and now he is not sure what he has missed. 'Neplokho', 'not bad', is about as high as Barinov's praise goes, so enjoy it. See you next time!
